transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you. Could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, Dr. Smith, I'm here because people keep acting like I'm imagining it. It’s very frustrating. I mean, just Tuesday I was doing the floors over at the Miller house—they have this gorgeous original hardwood, the kind you absolutely can't use regular mop water on, you have to use a special oil soap or it leaves these awful cloudy streaks. Mrs. Miller is so picky about her baseboards, too, she'll run a white cloth right over them just to check my work. 

But anyway, I know the hospital people and some folks from the agency have been watching our house. They think I don't notice them watching my cleaning routes, but I do. I take the 42 bus to get to my afternoon clients, and the bus driver always takes extra long at the stops. My husband used to take that same bus line years ago when he was still working at the plant. I used to pack him those little ham and cheese sandwiches he liked so much, with the mustard on the side so the bread wouldn't get soggy... 

But yes, they're watching my routes to see if I'm taking proper care of my husband. I know exactly what they're up to, even if everyone else says I'm making it up.
Do you ever hear any voices or sounds that other people around you cannot hear?

Well, yes, actually. I do. Even when the house is completely quiet—and I mean completely quiet, like late at night when the neighborhood settles down. We live on a cul-de-sac, you know, so we don't get much through traffic, except for the mailman and occasionally that teenager next door with the loud muffler on his Honda. I told his mother about that muffler, it's a real nuisance when I'm trying to get my resting time in between my morning and afternoon cleaning shifts. 

But anyway, when it's quiet like that, I hear this woman's voice. She's right near the kitchen window. Clear as day, like she's standing right there next to the sink. The sink is stainless steel, by the way, I polish it every Sunday with Bar Keepers Friend, it's the only thing that gets the water spots out. But she tells me to check the locks or to move my husband's pills. Just speaking right to me. I always keep his pills in that little daily organizer box, the one with the days of the week on it, but she tells me to move them. It's very clear.
Have you ever experienced periods where your mood was so low that you couldn't get out of bed, or periods where you felt so energetic and high that you didn't need to sleep?

Well, getting out of bed has never been a problem for me, really. I have to be up early for my morning clients. But there are definitely stretches where I just feel... bright, you know? Like I'm so strong and I can handle absolutely everything. I'll get through three houses in a day and still have energy to scrub my own baseboards. I use this little toothbrush for the corners—an old one, of course, I run it through the dishwasher first to sanitize it. My husband thinks I'm crazy for doing that, but you wouldn't believe the dust that gathers right where the trim meets the floor. 

But during those times, when I feel so full of energy, I do notice that if my husband questions me about something, or if one of my clients tries to tell me how to do my job—like Mrs. Miller trying to tell me about dusting the ceiling fans when I've been doing it for ten years—I just snap. I snap much harder than I mean to. I don't know why, it's like a wire gets pulled too tight. My husband's sister used to get like that, actually. She lived over in Dayton and she'd call on Sundays and just yell about the most random things, like how the grocery store bagged her canned goods. I always tell the baggers at the Piggly Wiggly to put the cans in double plastic, otherwise the handles just tear right through... but yes, I do get very snappy when I'm feeling that bright and energetic.

During those times when you feel that 'bright' energy and find yourself snapping at people, do the voices you hear happen at the same time, or do you hear them even when your mood is completely normal?

Well, they definitely happen at the same time, but... no, actually, it's not just when I'm feeling all wound up. There was this stretch recently, maybe a few weeks ago, where things were actually pretty quiet with me. I was sleeping a lot more, taking it easy, not rushing around to get all the houses done in one day. I even let my husband make his own lunch a few times, which he usually messes up—he puts the mayonnaise right on the bread and then wonders why it gets soggy by noon. I've told him a hundred times to put a piece of lettuce between the bread and the wet ingredients, it creates a barrier, you see. That's a trick I learned from this catering lady I used to clean for over in Westlake. She had this massive commercial refrigerator in her garage, took me two hours just to wipe down the stainless steel on that thing... 

But anyway, even during that quieter spell when I was resting more, I still heard that woman's voice right by the kitchen window. Clear as anything. And I still knew the agency was watching us, keeping tabs on my routes. So it doesn't really matter if I'm feeling bright or if I'm just taking it easy, they're still there.
